title: The Evolution of Automation at Google
subtitle: Move from scripts toward owned, observable, autonomous systems
summary: Pip’s automation repairs replicas faster than people can—and could spread a mistake just as quickly. The crew keeps domain teams responsible for management contracts, distinguishes scripted steps from autonomous lifecycle behavior, and validates scope before any large action.

concepts.title: Automation provides more than saved minutes
concepts.body: Pip finds three slightly different manual failover procedures. Software can execute one tested procedure consistently, quickly, repeatedly, and with measurements. Centralizing implementation also centralizes defects as well as fixes. Pip weighs recovery time and repeatability against development cost and the risk of applying a mistake at scale.

concepts.title: Autonomy changes the system boundary
concepts.body: Pip still has to notice failure and start the replacement script. Autonomy detects conditions and performs lifecycle actions without that trigger. Borg changes the boundary: applications request resources instead of owning permanent machines. Pip treats scheduling and replacement as system behavior, not a pile of host-specific repair scripts.

concepts.title: Service ownership keeps automation relevant
concepts.body: Pip’s central turnup script assumes an obsolete storage configuration. Automation decays when maintainers are detached from service changes and operation. Service teams owning management APIs let orchestration use stable contracts while implementations evolve. Pip returns storage turnup expertise to the team that actually changes storage.

concepts.title: Resumability and bounded effects
concepts.body: Pip’s repair workflow resumes after a partial run. Idempotency avoids extra effects on repetition, but stale checks or ambiguous targets remain dangerous. The chapter’s erasure failure treated an empty selection as all machines. Pip requires explicit scope, rejects empty targets, limits change rate, and exposes state before automation can amplify a mistake.

misconceptions.claim: An idempotent fix makes any surrounding workflow safe.
misconceptions.correction: Stale observations, dependencies, and ambiguous target selection can still make the workflow unsafe.

misconceptions.claim: A central automation team can permanently replace service-team ownership.
misconceptions.correction: Without service expertise and maintenance incentives, automation can drift away from the system it controls.

scenario.title: Replace hand-run deployment steps
scenario.context: A release requires copying artifacts, editing configuration, and restarting three services in order. One step was skipped last month. The release team has one afternoon to improve it.

options.label: Automate the sequence with checkpoints
options.benefit: The repeatable path reduces omission risk and leaves evidence of each step.
options.cost: Automation must handle partial completion and rollback.
options.consequence: A staged tool validates artifacts and stops safely between services.

options.label: Add a longer runbook
options.benefit: The runbook can clarify unusual recovery without code changes.
options.cost: Human execution remains error-prone under time pressure.
options.consequence: The runbook helps today, but the same manual toil returns next release.

scenario.debrief: A checkpoint records partial progress but does not by itself make retries safe. Validate each transition, make repeated operations safe, and expose the state needed to recover when the workflow stops.

quiz.question: What architectural change made Borg more than a collection of host scripts?
options: It treated the cluster as schedulable resources behind a management interface
It assigned each service a permanent host
It required operators to approve every restart
quiz.explanation: Scheduling and lifecycle management became intrinsic platform behavior.

quiz.question: Why did separating cluster turnup from service-owning teams eventually hurt automation?
options: It made every operation too idempotent
It prevented any reuse of code
Service changes stopped being reflected reliably in the automation
quiz.explanation: The team feeling turnup failures no longer had the relevant ownership and expertise.

quiz.question: A retry produces an empty list of machines to erase. What is the safe interpretation?
options: Erase every machine because the filter is absent
Perform no erasure and validate the intended scope
Reuse the largest previously seen list
quiz.explanation: Empty must not silently expand destructive scope; the chapter’s incident demonstrates that failure mode.

exercise.title: Make a partial workflow safe to resume
exercise.prompt: Design a service-turnup operation that may stop after configuration is created but before the service is ready. Specify ownership and retry behavior.
